### F1 · Letter §Major 1 · adapt · open
- **Finding:** The essay names layer 2 the hard case, credits Anthropic's mandatory-testing proposal, loads *Areopagitica* twice, and runs its test only on the Order's classified benchmarking (easy pass) and on its own layer-4/5 boundary (easy fail for its own side). The seven questions also have an uncited predecessor in Sastry et al. 2024. A pass on the Lieu–Moran Kill Switch Act would answer the "shield for one side" charge.
- **Rationale:** The diagnosis is right and the second reader reached it independently from the text alone. The prescription (write the paragraph; cite Sastry; state what the questions add; show a pass on a real safety bill) is right in outline, but the *content* of the paragraph is the author's, and the direction of the resolution is an identity-level fork the letter itself lists as open question 1 (F73). The editor's reading of the essay's premises (passes Q1, Q3, and Q5 in the near term; strains Q4 and Q7; acceptable only under Q6 conditions, a threshold not defined by what users ask, and no enforcement at layer 4) is, on my own re-reading of §VI, §X and §XII, what the premises actually yield; so it is adopted as the conservative option because it preserves the essay's existing commitments (the §X concession that a model that acts is conduct; the credit given to testing; the falsification clause's "unsigned weights a legal hazard" as the layer-4 sign).
- **Planned change:** Move M16: a new paragraph at l.266 running the eight questions on capability-conditioned pre-release testing of open-weight release, naming what it passes, what it strains, and what a version that passed would need, and locating the point at which a layer-2 rule becomes the Stationers' bargain (signature enforcement at the point of execution). Sastry cited at l.238 with one sentence on what the questions add (M15). The Kill Switch Act tested and passed in the same paragraph (M16), with its DHS shutdown order flagged under Q6.

### F7 · Letter §Major 3(d); second read (ii) · adapt · open *(pending Phase 1)*
- **Finding:** The diary was in the writer's desk; the cognitive record is in the provider's datacenter, and US law has treated that difference as dispositive for fifty years (Smith, Miller; narrowed by Carpenter and, on June 29, 2026, Chatrie). A prompt to a hosted service is a communication to a corporation; letters to lawyers, confessions, and library records each earned a doctrine explaining why disclosure to a counterparty did not waive confidentiality, and the essay proposes none.
- **Rationale:** Diagnosis right, and it is a gap in the argument, not the citations. Adapt: the essay's structural reply is better than a proposed privilege. It should (a) say the law is deciding, warrant by warrant, whether the medium of deliberation is a bank record or a home, and that Carpenter and Chatrie show the doctrine bending toward "indispensable and revealing" media, which is the essay's own description of the object; (b) claim what the privacy literature lacks: a warrant requirement governs *access* and touches neither retention nor classification nor referral, which is where the four conditions live; and (c) answer the second reader's "no doctrine" with the essay's actual answer, that the doctrine the record needs is partly architectural (what is kept, for how long, by whom) and only partly juridical, which is why the essay turns from the right to the architecture. A full privilege proposal is a different essay; recorded as deferred within this row.
- **Planned change:** M8 (three or four sentences after l.86); M17 (the four conditions as the retention/classification/referral question).
